newsitem.title: UK: Little chance of President Ramos getting 2nd term.
newsitem.headline: Little chance of President Ramos getting 2nd term.

text.p: One of the Philippines most powerful politicians on Thursday effectively ruled out any chance of President Fidel Ramos running for a second term, but declined to throw his own hat into the ring just yet.
An unofficial campaign has been under way to change the constitutional ban on anyone being president for more than one six-year term, which in the case of Ramos expires in just over a year.
"It's next to impossible to pull it off," visiting House of Representatives Speaker Jose de Venecia told Reuters in an interview.
The strength of opinion on either side of the debate would make a change in the constitution too divisive and anyway there was hardly any time left to make the amendment, he added.
The 68-year old Ramos, whose administration is widely credited with turning around the fortunes of the Philippines, has denied any plans to get the rules changed.

De Venecia was wary about predicting who might be his eventual replacement, but warned that Vice President Joseph Estrada, who is generally seen as the man to beat in 1998, was not necessarily the front-runner.
De Venecia was also coy about expressing his own presidential hopes.
"I'm not declaring now...If I do that, it's good bye to all this legislation (to push through Congress)," he said.
Crucial tax reforms are currently being debated in Congress and de Venecia hoped they would get final approval by the end of May.
That would be in time for the end of 34 years of International Monetary Fund supervision of the country's economy.
The Philippines hopes that its escape from the clutches of the IMF will firmly establish its credentials as one of the "tiger" economies in Asia.
There are three simultaneous changes the country had to institute -- modernise its agriculture, turn into an industrial state and move into the information age, de Venecia said.
"Then we can overtake Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, leading the region and competing with the economic tigers of East Asia."
